html: The preceding subsection established the basal ganglia’s error architecture: phasic dopamine as a structured, distributional, multi-timescale evaluative broadcast, sculpted by cholinergic dynamics and routed across parallel cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops. But an error signal does not by itself change policy. For the basal ganglia, learning occurs only when that evaluative signal is converted into persistent changes in synaptic—and, in some cases, intrinsic—gain at the circuit elements that actually participated in action selection. Dopamine, in other words, is not itself the update; it is the teaching variable that opens, biases, or closes plasticity windows at eligible synapses. The central question of BG plasticity is therefore not merely what the error signal means, but where, when, and under what local conditions it can write. The answer is a family of pathway-specific, neuromodulator-gated, multi-factor rules centered above all on glutamatergic inputs to spiny projection neurons, where cortical and thalamic state representations, dopaminergic reinforcement, cholinergic timing signals, postsynaptic depolarization, dendritic nonlinearities, and retrograde signaling are integrated into lasting changes in action value, policy bias, and habit structure. Because the general logic of Hebbian, STDP, three-factor, and related plasticity rules was developed in The Fundamentals, the aim here is narrower: to specify the basal-ganglia-specific biological substrate and learning rules that close the loop from evaluative error to durable policy optimization
